annotation: A collaborative study joining archaeology, archives and community memories. It offers twentieth-century Oklahoma history and a clear explanation of its methods. The authors distinguish community priorities and quoted memories from their own academic interpretation.

Raw interviews, field notes and spatial datasets are held by named offices and may be accessible only at their discretion; none were requested or accessed. title: A Terrible Truth: The Tonkawa Massacre of 1862
author: Joseph Connole
publisher: Chronicles of Oklahoma, 97(4), Winter 2019–2020, pp. 450–467; Oklahoma Historical Society / Gateway to Oklahoma History, UNT Libraries
annotation: An 18-page article in the Oklahoma Historical Society’s scholarly journal. Connole compares explanations for the 1862 attack and argues that long-running political alliances and failures of federal and Confederate protection shaped the Tonkawa’s vulnerability. This is the author’s secondary interpretation, not a Tonkawa-authored account or a settled consensus; his own opening discussion says the instigators and immediate reasons remain unclear.
contentReviewScope: Complete article body, printed pp. 450–465, and selected endnotes pp. 466–467 inspected from the UNT/Oklahoma Historical Society digital copy. The author relies on cited historical scholarship and government reports; most cited underlying records were not independently re-read in this pass. The article notes one known first-hand account of the Fort Cobb attack. Its casualty estimate and causal interpretation remain attributed. The map and archival photograph were not separately inspected.

annotation: This 2010 Spanish-language book chapter surveys Kickapoo histories from the Great Lakes to Coahuila and Texas and discusses the formation of the Texas community, cross-border relations, land, federal recognition, and the Lucky Eagle casino context. title: Ethnic Consciousness in Cultural Survival: The Morongo Band of Mission Indians and the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas
publisher: Elisabeth A. Mager; translation by Heather Dashner Monk; American Indian Culture and Research Journal / eScholarship, University of California
annotation: This peer-reviewed comparative study includes a dedicated section on the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas and El Nacimiento. Mager identifies documentary research, participant observation, and interviews as methods and cites interviews conducted from 1995 to 2015, along with the Texas Tribe’s 1981–1984 Land Acquisition Committee report. Selected passages discuss land acquisition and economic history; the author’s theory of “ethnic consciousness,” causal claims, and generalizations remain her interpretation, not a community consensus. This is the same researcher represented by sources 6 and 11, so repeated claims are not independent corroboration. Cultural descriptions outside the selected historical scope were not used.

title: No-ko-aht’s Talk: A Kickapoo Chief’s Account of a Tribal Journey from Kansas to Mexico and Return in the Sixties
publisher: George A. Root, editor; Kansas Historical Society; account recorded by Franklin G. Adams
annotation: The article prints a May 31, 1867 account attributed to Kickapoo leader No-ko-aht and recorded in shorthand by federal agent Franklin G. Adams. No-ko-aht describes travel between Kansas and Mexico, the 1865 Dove Creek conflict, life in Coahuila, and his objections to treaty pressure and settler encroachment. This is a historically valuable but mediated account: the recorder was a federal agent, George A. Root edited and published it in 1932, and the surrounding editorial narrative uses period terminology and makes claims that should not be adopted as neutral fact. The printed account and editorial summary also differ in chronology and group counts; the discrepancy is retained rather than reconciled here.
publicationDate: Interview recorded May 31, 1867; edited/published February 1932, Kansas Historical Quarterly 1(2), pp. 153–159
contentReviewScope: Full transcribed article and footnotes read, pp.153–159. Inspected the editor’s account and the attributed No-ko-aht statement; no independent corroboration of every event, date, casualty number, or quotation was established.
accessNotes: Public transcription hosted by Kansas Historical Society; source page states digitized with permission. Historical spellings, editorial framing, and one illegible passage are retained as source limitations.

author: Grand Portage Band of Lake Superior Chippewa
publisher: Grand Portage Band of Lake Superior Chippewa
type: Tribal news release / contemporary land stewardship
contentReviewScope: Read the full 83-line public Band news release on October 23, 2026. annotation: A Grand Portage Band news release reports that a February 2026 acquisition restored three parcels totaling about 87 acres to Band ownership through a partnership with the Lloyd K. Johnson Foundation and Minnesota Land Trust. The Band describes three distinct routes by which those parcels left Band ownership: 1854 treaty cession, state school-trust transfer, and allotment. This is a direct community source for the Bands current action and its historical interpretation; the underlying treaty, land-title chain, tax records, and allotment documents were not independently checked. The Bands broad discussion of allotment policy remains attributed to the release and is not generalized to every Ojibwe Band. A linked map/images package is not included.

title: Presidio Los Adaes: Spanish, French, and Caddoan Interaction on the Northern Frontier
publisher: Historical Archaeology 38(3), pp. 65–77 · Society for Historical Archaeology; authorized Texas Beyond History copy
author: H. F. Gregory, George Avery, Aubra L. Lee, and Jay C. Blaine
annotation: Actual scanned article visually inspected at printed pp. 65, 67–71, and 74–75, including the excavation overview and conclusions. Compares documentary expectations with Indigenous pottery, French and Spanish goods, architecture, and food remains at the presidio. Material patterns concern a mixed colonial settlement; they do not identify every maker as Adai or prove equal power and universal harmony. Site-specific counts and social interpretations need their original contexts. This authored journal study is distinct from the later public exhibit.

title: El sistema fonológico del Kickapoo de Coahuila analizado desde las metodologías distribucional y funcional
publisher: José Luis Moctezuma Zamarrón and Fernando Nava López; Instituto Nacional de Lenguas Indígenas (INALI)
annotation: A substantial Spanish-language study combines a short ethnographic overview of the El Nacimiento community with two phonological analyses of the Coahuila variety and a chapter on a practical writing system. The author reports six months of fieldwork in 1980–1983 and later visits in 1988 and 2010; a later chapter describes consultation and community decision-making in developing a practical alphabet. These are dated, author-attributed observations, not a measure of present language use or a universal account of every Kickapoo community. Restricted cultural descriptions were excluded from the atlas synthesis.

title: Leech Lake Band of Chippewa Indians v. Herbst, 334 F. Supp. 1001 (D. Minn. 1971)
author: U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota, Chief Judge Edward J. Devitt
publisher: Justia, reproducing a reported federal district-court opinion
sourceKind: Reported U.S. District Court memorandum and order
topics: Treaty fishing, hunting, and wild-rice rights
annotation: The complete reported opinion addresses whether Leech Lake Band members could fish, hunt, and gather wild rice on public lands and waters within the Leech Lake Reservation free from Minnesota game and fish laws. The court held that treaty rights had not been abrogated by the Nelson Act and declared those activities protected on the specified public lands and waters. The opinion did not accept the Band’s claim to exclusive regulatory authority over all fishing, hunting, and ricing. This is a dated judicial holding in a particular case, not a statement of current regulations or a substitute for later law.
contentReviewScope: Read the full opinion and notes (reported text at pages 1001–1010; Justia lines 38–143). The opinion recounts the litigants’ positions, testimony, treaty/legal analysis, and the court’s narrow declaratory judgment. The 1855/1864/1867 treaty originals, trial exhibits, and later proceedings were not independently inspected in this entry.

title: State v. Forge, 262 N.W.2d 341 (Minn. 1977)
author: Supreme Court of Minnesota
publisher: Justia, reproducing a reported Minnesota Supreme Court opinion
annotation: The full opinion recounts the Leech Lake Band’s 1969 federal lawsuit, the 1971 Herbst decision, the 1973 settlement and consent judgment, and challenges to Minnesota’s reservation fishing stamp. The Minnesota Supreme Court held that Minnesota Chippewa Tribe members retained treaty rights and upheld the 1973 statutory compromise and the convictions of nonmembers who fished without the stamp. This later ruling supplies important historical context for the 1971 opinion; it does not establish every present-day regulation or decide all treaty-right questions.

title: Fond du Lac Band of Lake Superior Chippewa v. Cummins et al., Document 48 (D. Minn. Feb. 24, 2023)
author: United States District Court for the District of Minnesota; Chief Judge Patrick J. Schiltz
publisher: Justia, reproducing the federal district-court order
sourceKind: District-court order denying a motion to dismiss
annotation: In a challenge to a Forest Service land exchange for the proposed NorthMet mine, the District Court denied PolyMet’s motion to dismiss. At this pleading-stage ruling, it accepted the complaint’s allegation that the exchange could remove access to 6,650 acres used for the Band’s treaty rights and held that the Band had standing to assert its own 1854 Treaty usufructuary interests; those rights were not exclusively individual member rights. This is not a decision on the merits of the land exchange or the ultimate project outcome. The alleged access loss is described as a complaint allegation, not a factual finding.
contentReviewScope: Read the full 18-page opinion as reproduced on Justia, including the docket/date and disposition (lines 38–50), the complaint’s background and stated alleged injury (lines 51–63), the treaty and tribal-right analysis (lines 64–98), and the order denying dismissal (lines 103–110). The complaint and docket exhibits, Forest Service Record of Decision, environmental review, and later case history were not independently inspected.

title: Materials Related to the Co-Management of the Chippewa National Forest: The Right to Self-Governance — Historical and Current Overview of the Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe
author: Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe, Division of Resource Management
publicationDate: Undated compilation; contains a 2019 Memorandum of Understanding and a 2020 briefing presentation
annotation: A first-party Leech Lake Band educational and resource-management account, created to explain historical events, treaties, the Band’s government, and its agency relationships to Band staff and citizens. The historical overview narrates the 1837, 1854, 1855, 1864, and 1867 treaty sequence, later allotment and logging, the 1898 Sugar Point conflict, and the Band’s resource-governance work. Treaty-right and legal conclusions are presented as the Band’s institutional interpretation; the underlying treaty instruments, court opinions, and cited historical records were not independently checked in this source review. The booklet also includes later co-management materials that should be read as dated documents, not assumed to describe every current policy.
contentReviewScope: Read the complete first 20-page “Right to Self-Governance: Historical and Current Overview” (PDF pages 4–23), including its preface, treaty chronology, Nelson Act/allotment and timber discussion, Sugar Point account, present governance and federal/state-agency relationships. The complete PDF has 133 pages; later slide decks, the 2019 MOU, appendices, management letters, implementation guide, and species list were not inspected as separate works. No map or sensitive site information was reused.

title: The Caddo Indians of Louisiana — second edition, The Adaes section
publisher: Louisiana Division of Archaeology · Anthropological Study No. 2
author: Clarence H. Webb and Hiram F. Gregory
annotation: Inspected the cover, reissue foreword, historical context, and The Adaes section on PDF pp. 22–24. The foreword says this edition largely reissues a 1978 text. A substantial, explicitly Adai-focused account considers dispersed settlement, mission connections, pottery, and possible village identifications. Several sites and affiliations are hypotheses. Its confident Caddoan classification and colonial mission dates require comparison with later specialists; regional archaeological periods do not date the origin of the Adai people. Sensitive locations and funerary details are not reproduced.

annotation: Selected methodological pages explain the author’s reorganization of earlier vocabulary lists and discuss disputed language classifications. author: Lorenda Belone, Ardena Orosco, Eloise Damon, Willymae Smith-McNeal, Rebecca Rae, Mingma L. Sherpa, Orrin B. Myers, Anslem O. Omeh, and Nina Wallerstein; coauthors include Mescalero Apache Prevention Program and System of Care staff
publisher: Public Health Reviews 38 (2017), article 30; University of New Mexico and Mescalero Apache community partnership; PubMed Central open-access copy
annotation: A peer-reviewed article coauthored by University of New Mexico researchers and staff affiliated with the Mescalero Apache Prevention Program and System of Care. It reports that the Tribe requested the partnership, that a Tribal Council resolution supported co-writing and co-submission, and that a Mescalero Apache Tribal Research Team adapted and piloted a family program. The authors state the manuscript received Tribal Council and Southwest Tribal IRB approval. The study concerns a specific 2013–2014 pilot, not current program availability, all Mescalero families, or long-term outcomes. Its brief historical statements—including a broad homeland context spanning parts of Texas, Arizona and Mexico—remain attributed to the article; the underlying historical records were not checked here. The Atlas does not reproduce curriculum materials, participant data, images, or private content.
contentReviewScope: Read the open-access article body: publication metadata, abstract, research-partnership and historical-background sections, team formation and curriculum adaptation, pilot design and sample, selected results, discussion/conclusion, acknowledgments, approval statement and data-availability note (visible sections around lines 33–160, 176–215, 224–300 and 373). The pilot is discussed only as a dated collaborative research project; small sample, incomplete follow-up, short duration, and the authors’ statement that no difference in substance use was observed are kept in view. No participant-level data, session materials, images or follow-up study results were accessed. Cited historical works were not independently reviewed.

title: Idaho v. United States, 533 U.S. 262
publisher: Supreme Court of the United States
annotation: Read the opinion in volume 533, pp. 262–280 (bound PDF pp. 265–280 in an 868-page volume). The Court held that the United States holds in trust for the Tribe the specified submerged lands within the reservation, including portions of the lake and river. The holding is limited to title in the disputed submerged lands; it is not a ruling that the Tribe owns the whole lake or every basin interest.

publisher: Texas History Trust, Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest
annotation: The printed treaty text lists Alabama and Coushatta among groups it calls Cherokee “associate Bands” and proposes that the named bands form one community within specified bounds. This is a Republic of Texas diplomatic document in colonial/state language, mediated through a later edited transcription. Its text does not establish that the proposed agreement was ratified, implemented, or accepted as a lasting boundary by the named peoples. It is not a present homeland map.
contentReviewScope: Transcript of the February 23, 1836 document on printed pages 14–15 of volume I reviewed through the Texas History Trust/University of North Texas text. The treaty’s opening and land-boundary article were inspected; the full volume, manuscript original, signatures and implementation record were not reviewed.
publicationDate: Document dated February 23, 1836; edited volume issued 1995

author: Memorial adopted by the Tonkawa Tribe at Oakland Agency on January 2, 1907; member affidavits and historical extracts appended
type: Primary community petition and member testimony in a congressional record
publicationDate: Memorial adopted January 2, 1907; presented to Senate January 28, 1908
annotation: This six-page Senate document reproduces a memorial adopted by the Tonkawa Tribe in council and affidavits from members contesting the 1891 cession’s terms and the way it was negotiated. Their claims are direct evidence of the Tribe’s later position and named members’ recollections, not a judicial finding or independent valuation. The memorial’s account should be read alongside the 1892 federal document, which records commissioners’ contrasting assessment. It also reprints older federal agent reports with their own colonial and comparative framing; those passages are attributed rather than adopted.
contentReviewScope: Read all six PDF pages, including the council memorial, affidavits by Frank E. Mason, John Rush Buffalo, and John Allen, and appended excerpts from federal agents’ reports. Claims about the negotiation are attributed to the memorialists and affiants; the appended agent language is not treated as Tonkawa testimony. No individualized allotment or burial site details were published.

author: U.S. House of Representatives; correspondence by War Department, Interior Department, and Army officers
publisher: U.S. Government Publishing Office, Congressional Serial Set; digitized by the Law Library of Congress
type: Primary government correspondence / Congressional Serial Set document
contentReviewScope: Read the full searchable text of the eight-page public PDF, including its letters and reports dated 1872–1876. annotation: The congressional document records federal officials’ accounts of a small Lipan group moving from Fort Sill to Fort Griffin in 1874, subsequent ration decisions affecting Tonkawa and Lipan people there, and proposed removal options. The 1875 Interior Department letter reports kinship through intermarriage and discusses a possible consolidation; it is an official’s account and recommendation, not a Lipan-authored history or evidence that the proposal was implemented. It must not be generalized to all Lipan people or treated as proof of incorporation into Mescalero Apache.

title: The Battle of Dove Creek
publisher: William C. Pool; Southwestern Historical Quarterly / Texas State Historical Association; The Portal to Texas History, University of North Texas Libraries
annotation: Pool’s 19-page article reconstructs the January 8, 1865 Dove Creek battle using military correspondence and other records.
